newsitem.title: USA: New products - Science magazine for children.
newsitem.headline: New products - Science magazine for children.

text.p: Kids have an innate love of science, questioning from day one where they come from, why birds fly and why the sky is blue.
But schools often "give a fixed prejudice that science is boring," dampening youngsters' enthusiasm at an early age, the editor of a new children's magazine says.
Trying to counter this, the Cricket Magazine Group, of Peru, Ill., has published a new glossy science magazine aimed at kids aged 6-14, named Muse.
"Kids have a lot of fundamental questions about the world. It's our conviction to explain it correctly," said Andre Carus, editor-in-chief.
Many magazines, television and video programmes are designed to entertain children, but Carus said, "we have taken an interest in trying to do more than that.
"It's our own conviction that if it's explained correctly" children love science, Carus said.

Muse offers its readers a bit of whimsy along with the facts. For example, in a piece on the ancient muses, such as Clio (history) and Thalia (comedy), there's Bo, the muse of "factoids" and Mimi, the muse of "getting along with people," drawn in cartoon style.
"We're interested in doing controversial topics, things that make kids think," said Bob Harper, Muse publisher.
Such topics might include vegetarianism, with a look at ethical and nutritional issues involved in eating animal protein.

When dealing with the topic of evolution, and the pressure in some sectors to give equal time to Creationism, Harper said, "We are representing the scientific community on this. We won't say the Creation issue should be on par with evolution."
In the premire issue, Muse looks at life on Mars, "not a subtle topic," Harper said.

Writing that scientists believe that Mars was home to simple bacteria-like organisms, Muse adds, "Of course, bacteria are a long way from intelligent aliens. And there is absolutely no sign that more complex life forms -- like plants, animals or people -- ever evolved on Mars.
"Then again, bacteria was the only form of life on Earth until 500 million years ago."

Balancing what could be described as serious information are line-drawn characters, similar to the characters that graced the margins of the children's magaine, Cricket, for the last 23 years. Like Woodstock in the Peanuts comic strips, these characters add funny, sometimes curious, observations.

The magazine will be published every two months "so we can do it very well," Harper said. He said it is difficult to describe science in a "very complete way" and the magazine's editors have taken great pains to find writers "who can translate complicated sources for kids."
Muse is a joint project with the Smithsonian Institution, and each of the bi-monthly issues will contain something from the Smithsonian collection.

The first, January, 1997, issue introduces readers to Dr. Doug Ubelaker, a forensic anthropologist at the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History, who can look at bones and tell where the person came from, how old they were and how they got to be that way. A lot of his work is with the FBI and police.
Other articles in this issue look at the Rosetta Stone, which had inscriptions in Greek and ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, and one of the stone's translators, Jean-Francois Champollion.
The articles are written so that younger children will not be scared away, and so that older children will not be bored.
"There are kids out there that don't want it boiled down," Harper said.
"Some (adults) bemoan the fact that kids don't read, but we cater to kids who do read and look at reading as one way to learn."
No, he said, Muse is not in competition with computers and the education and entertainment they can provide.
After all, "you can't use a computer unless you can read," he said.
Muse, published every two months, costs $4.95 an issue on selected newsstands and is available by subscription at $22 for six issues.
To order or get more information, call 1-800-827-0227.
